title: Transient Information Effect https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11251-015-9362-9
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 15, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers a study by Leahy and Sweller testing when the multimedia 'modality effect' (audio-visual beats visual-only) holds up and when it reverses, using a task where students had to interpret contour maps. When the accompanying verbal information was short and simple, audio-visual presentation was better, as the classic modality effect predicts. But when the verbal information was longer and more complex, that advantage shrank and eventually reversed — visual-only presentation with written text outperformed audio-visual, because spoken information is transient and students can't revisit it the way they can re-read text. Barton draws the practical rule: match modality to length and complexity, defaulting to audio-visual for short, simple verbal content and switching to written text once the verbal load gets long or complex, since sentence length itself is a rough proxy for how much element interactivity — and thus cognitive load — a passage carries.
points: The multimedia modality effect (audio-visual beats visual-only) only holds when verbal information is short and simple — it shrinks and eventually reverses as verbal complexity and length increase.

Spoken information is transient: students cannot easily revisit and reprocess it the way they can re-read written text, which is why long or complex verbal explanations should default to written form.

Sentence length is a usable rough proxy for element interactivity — longer sentences tend to signal higher cognitive load, so teachers should aim for clear, concise language especially in spoken instruction.
The practical rule is modality-matching: use audio-visual presentation for short, simple verbal content, and switch to visual-only written text once information becomes lengthy or complex.
quotes: Our results suggest that when dealing with multiple sources of information that refer to each other and cannot be understood in isolation, presenting the information in an audio-visual format is likely to be beneficial providing that verbal information is relatively simple and short.

As verbal information increases in complexity and length, the advantage of audio-visual information decreases and eventually reverses. At that point verbal information should be presented in written form
This is due to the transient nature of spoken information. Students cannot easily revisit and process the information as they can with written text.
Sentence length can be used as an indicator of element interactivity. Longer sentences often indicate higher element interactivity, which can increase cognitive load.
Teachers should consider the complexity and length of verbal information when deciding whether to use an audio-visual or visual-only format.
